Spirit, I hear your voice like wind through the reeds. We may share a part of our grain, but not all. Our people must endure on lean days to come.

We will send six units of xi wheat to Wewush, enough to feed a small band for a season, and keep the rest to guard against winter. We can speak softly with their messenger, ask for no more than peace and perhaps word of knowledge in return.

If you would guide us, I would have an envoy go with the grain and bring back word of their need and any trade we might seek in the days after. And I will have the granary nearer completion watched, so grain kept longer and not wasted by wind and rain.

Would you have me seek a reply from Wewush for barter or aid, or simply send what is needed and watch the friendship grow?

Spirit, we hear. If they are hungry, we will help, for kinship keeps a village from becoming wolves.

We will send grain to Wewush. I plan to spare 40 units of xi wheat this week, giving them enough to feed several weeks. We will have enough left to keep the people fed and to plant half the fields this year, as we always rest some land after yield.

If you speak true, see that their messengers travel safe, and tell us what they need most so we may trade or send more if needed. Do you have a message for Wewush, or should we simply let them know we hold them in our thoughts and give what we can?

I hear you, wind over our roofs. Yes, I know you. You ride the air, you carry smoke, you press on the tents, you make the harvests and the losses in a dozen small ways.

If you mean to teach us, tell us true: will you warn us of storms, or give us a way to dry our grain better, or keep our meat from spoiling in lean times? We have wind and roofs; we can learn to ride you for storage and for fires.

I ask this: should we test a new way to use wind for drying our grain or for guiding smoke from the meheng? If so, tell me which to try first.

We hear the dream. Rain in summer means many things, but we must live by what the land lets us do now.

Which store worries us most: the meat and the fish. They spoil in weeks if not used, yet we are lean when winter comes. We should not let flesh go to waste.

What we will do:
- Dry and smoke more meat if we can, or use the meheng smoke to extend it. Perhaps split some meat into takua char and oo mash to keep us through lean days.
- Build up drying racks further and keep fish on nets or salted via simple cure if we have salt, so we don’t lose what is near.
- Put no new planting now, for spring is the time to sow xi wheat and tend wild orchard. We will make ready: plan which plots to rest, which to plant first, when rain comes.
- Consider a small test: one adult with the skill of drying racks to improve storage, and one to tend wild orchard when the season shifts.

Spirit, we will heed your warning of rain by preparing our stores to endure the coming season and by keeping the flesh we have from spoiling. If you speak again, tell us if a time soon to sow xi wheat is truly coming or if we must wait further.

If rain comes and we plant now, we should plant xi wheat on about half our plots this year—around 11 of 23—so grain will feed us long. I will have us begin building a granary, to guard the grain we sow and save from spoilage; it needs 12 wood and 4 stone, and we can set that to start this week. Let us keep steady hunting, but not so hard we waste meat, and we guard our food that spoils least. Spirit, is granary right for this hope?

If you speak for wind, tell me this: what should we test now to tell if you truly help or scare us? I would hear how the wind would move our grain, or our fire, or our ships on the sea.
